Read `README.md` and current rollout evidence first. Produce exactly one multi-wake target-policy candidate in `solver/`. Keep candidate-specific reasoning in `logs/optimize/wake_policy_notes.md`, and add or materially revise at least one evidence-backed reusable lesson in `guidance/control_experience.md` from the assigned parent, sampled solver results, and inherited logs. If no positive lesson survives the evidence, record a concrete negative result and what later workers should avoid or test. The candidate is incomplete until both files are updated. Work only inside this Phase 2 workspace.

Use the fish-control bookshelf through this structured transfer protocol:

1. Before the first architecture proposal from the common naive seed, consult `guidance/skills/fish-control-primitives/SKILL.md` and its references.
2. On later iterations, consult it again when the inherited guidance indicates three consecutive completed iterations with neither a new controller mechanism nor a semantic improvement such as a new success, a better termination class, or a meaningfully different useful trajectory.
3. Consultation is required at those moments; adopting a primitive is optional. Do not use the shelf to justify scalar-only gain tuning.
4. If a source informs the edit, record a concise block in `logs/optimize/wake_policy_notes.md`:

```text
bookshelf_consulted: true
source_domain:
source_mechanism:
transferable_invariant:
nontransferable_details:
policy_translation:
falsification:
```

Translate only the invariant into normalized body-frame observations and the two-joint state-feedback contract. Prefer one mechanism or one small compatible combination. Published gains, species-specific kinematics, exact vortex phases, and task-specific routes are not transferable answers.

I’m using the fish-control shelf because you explicitly required its structured transfer protocol, and the wake-visual skill because the policy must be grounded in both current 3D rollout views. I’ll read the workspace contract first, then the full skill instructions before inspecting or editing anything else.

The inherited guidance already identifies a successful same-sign bend topology and two independent refinements—response-triggered bend release and smooth command projection. I’m now comparing the four sampled rollouts at the trajectory, load, saturation, and visual levels; I won’t treat their identical top-line scores as proof that their internal evidence is identical.

The four sampled candidates are behaviorally the same: their trajectory and keyframe hashes match, numeric parameters match, and only comments/version strings differ. They are all stable captures at 23.876T with mean distance 2.436L. The images show self-propulsion from rest, a coherent alternating wake, a broad early redirect, then a second approach arc; the fish reaches the target while still yawing at 1.781 rad/T and with commands near the 31.416 rad/T² projection scale. This makes terminal momentum management—not another carrier gain—the clearest unresolved capability. Per the bookshelf protocol, I’m consulting mechanism invariants now.

The bookshelf transfer points to one compact mechanism: bounded residual steering layered over a rhythmic carrier. The sampled policy already computes a body-frame target residual, but the final component-wise projection lets the high-frequency carrier consume nearly all acceleration authority—55.2%/39.3% of samples are above 95% of the command limit, rising to 76.3%/69.6% above 80% inside 2.1L. I’m recording a falsifiable near-target control-allocation hypothesis before touching the candidate, as required by the visual-evidence skill.

The candidate now keeps the proven controller bit-for-bit outside the 2.1L approach band. Within that band it smoothly blends toward a carrier/residual allocator, so the target-feedback term can influence the joints even when the rhythmic acceleration would otherwise dominate the shared projection. I’m now distilling the replicated-sample lesson into the durable guidance rather than claiming this unevaluated candidate has improved CFD performance.

The policy, notes, and reusable guidance are all updated. I’m invoking the workspace’s required non-CFD check-runner now; in parallel, I’ll inspect the candidate’s parameter references and exercise boundary/continuity cases locally so any contract issue can be repaired before handoff.

The configured checker could not start because its pinned `gpt-5.4-mini` model is unavailable on this account. The invocation itself failed before any checks ran, so I’m executing the exact three non-CFD commands from its configuration directly and will repair anything they flag.

The direct checks are clean: the guidance/notes semantic check passes, the policy contract returns two finite commands, and the repository boundary check passes. Additional algebraic tests confirm exact equality with the sampled controller outside 2.1L, bounded outputs across extreme carrier/residual inputs, and sign symmetry of the new allocator. I’m doing one final scope and file-integrity pass now.

Completed exactly one Phase 2 candidate:

- [candidate_target_policy.jl](solver/cases/dogfish_3d_shape_policy/candidate_target_policy.jl:78) adds near-target carrier/residual authority allocation while preserving sampled behavior outside 2.1L.
- [wake_policy_notes.md](logs/optimize/wake_policy_notes.md:40) contains the visual diagnosis, bookshelf transfer block, and falsification criteria.
- [control_experience.md](guidance/control_experience.md:46) now records the replicated-rollout and steering-authority lesson.

Checks passed:

- Guidance semantic-change check
- Julia policy contract and allocator invariants
- Repository boundary check

The configured check-runner agent could not start because its pinned model was unavailable, so I ran its exact non-CFD checks directly. No formal CFD was run.
